reason: The Statement of Fundamental Truths never addresses the extent of the atonement (universal vs. definite). Article 5 states only that 'Man's only hope of redemption is through the shed blood of Jesus Christ,' which speaks to the ground of salvation, not its intended scope.

Article 3(c) lists 'His miracles' only as historical evidence of Christ's own deity (Acts 2:22; 10:38); it makes no claim about miracles in general or about the relationship between the miraculous and scientific method, which is what this position asserts.

No article addresses personal subjective revelation (impressions, dreams, an inward voice) as a category. Article 7 describes the baptism in the Holy Spirit's effects (power for service, reverence, consecration, love) but says nothing about God speaking directly to individuals today.
The existing citation ('general practice') was not a citation to the document at all. None of the 16 articles address personal devotional practice or spiritual disciplines.
Article 2 is entirely about the Trinity (the Godhead's relationship and unity); it does not address divine foreknowledge of free creaturely choices at all.
Same as above: Article 2 does not address the mechanism of God's foreknowledge; no other article does either.

Article 7 never mentions prophecy by name; it speaks generically of 'the gifts and their uses' with a bare cross-reference to 1 Corinthians 12. The specific claim here (congregational prophecy is fallible and must be weighed) is not stated anywhere in the document, as the position's own prior note already conceded.

Article 13 ('The Blessed Hope') describes only the future resurrection/translation of 'those who have fallen asleep in Christ'; no article states what happens to the soul between death and resurrection.
No article addresses the fate of those who die without hearing the gospel.
No article characterizes non-Christian religions as false or demonic, or addresses other religions at all.

No article singles out evangelism to Jewish people as a distinct question; Article 10's Great Commission language is entirely general and Article 14's mention of Israel is confined to the future millennial reign.
No article addresses the sovereignty/free-will mechanism of a person's response to grace.
No article uses or addresses 'election' or predestination in any form.
No article addresses apostasy or the possibility of forfeiting salvation, as the position's own prior note already conceded.

No article addresses whether assurance of final salvation is conditional on continuing faithfulness; Article 5(b) speaks only to present evidences of salvation (the Spirit's witness, a righteous life), not to the durability question this position answers.

Article 1 states Scripture is verbally inspired and the infallible, authoritative rule of faith and conduct; it says nothing about whether an ordinary reader can grasp it without a specially authorised interpreter.
Article 1 makes no statement about interpretive method (grammatical-historical or otherwise) or the Spirit's role in illumination.

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 3(d)
fields.note: The statement says: "His substitutionary work on the cross" (Article 3(d), citing 1 Corinthians 15:3 and 2 Corinthians 5:21) — the article on Christ's deity, not Article 5, is where the substitutionary language actually sits.

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 6(b)
fields.note: The statement says the Lord's Supper is "the symbol expressing our sharing the divine nature of our Lord Jesus Christ...a memorial of His suffering and death...and a prophecy of His second coming" (Article 6(b), Holy Communion, not Article 7).

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 8
fields.note: The statement says: "The baptism of believers in the Holy Spirit is witnessed by the initial physical sign of speaking with other tongues as the Spirit of God gives them utterance" (Article 8, The Initial Physical Evidence of the Baptism in the Holy Spirit — not Article 7, which is the baptism itself).

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 14
fields.note: The statement says: "The second coming of Christ includes the rapture of the saints...followed by the visible return of Christ with His saints to reign on the earth for one thousand years" (Article 14, The Millennial Reign of Christ — Article 15 is a different article, The Final Judgment).

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 14
fields.note: The statement says: "This millennial reign will bring the salvation of national Israel" (Article 14, The Millennial Reign of Christ — Article 15 is The Final Judgment, a different article).

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 13
fields.note: The statement says: "The resurrection of those who have fallen asleep in Christ and their translation together with those who are alive and remain unto the coming of the Lord is the imminent and blessed hope of the Church" (Article 13, The Blessed Hope — not Article 14, which is the millennial reign). The Statement affirms imminency but does not itself specify pretribulational timing or mention a seven-year tribulation; that specific sequencing is taught in the AG's separate 'The Rapture of the Church' position paper, which does not carry the Statement's binding weight.

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 15
fields.note: The statement says the unrepentant "will be consigned to everlasting punishment in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone, which is the second death" (Article 15, The Final Judgment — Article 16 is a different article, The New Heavens and the New Earth).

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 5
fields.note: The statement says: "Man's only hope of redemption is through the shed blood of Jesus Christ the Son of God" (Article 5, The Salvation of Man — not Article 3, which is about Christ's deity rather than salvation's exclusivity).

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 5(a)
fields.note: The statement says salvation comes "By the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Spirit, being justified by grace through faith" (Article 5(a)) — this affirms grace-through-faith justification, but the document never uses the five-solas framework itself (it does not, in this article, speak to Scripture alone or the glory of God alone), so this is the movement's broad theological alignment rather than a confessionally defined 'five solas' article.

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 8, contrasted with charismatic-stream teaching such as John Wimber, Power Evangelism (1985)
Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 2(f)-(g); Article 3
fields.note: The statement says: "He is, therefore, acknowledged to be both God and man; who because He is God and man, is 'Immanuel,' God with us" (Article 2(f)), and "The Lord Jesus Christ is the eternal Son of God" (Article 3, which lists His virgin birth, sinless life, miracles, substitutionary death, bodily resurrection and exaltation). The Statement affirms full deity and full humanity without using Chalcedon's own technical vocabulary.

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 3(a)
fields.note: The statement says: "His virgin birth" (Article 3(a), citing Matthew 1:23; Luke 1:31,35).

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 3(e)
fields.note: The statement says: "His bodily resurrection from the dead" (Article 3(e), citing Matthew 28:6; Luke 24:39; 1 Corinthians 15:4).

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Preamble
fields.note: The preamble says: "The Bible is our all-sufficient rule for faith and practice...The phraseology employed in this statement is not inspired or contended for, but the truth set forth is held to be essential to a full-gospel ministry." The Statement explicitly declines binding authority for its own wording, holding Scripture alone as the rule.

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 2
fields.note: The statement affirms Trinitarian content in its own propositional wording — "The one true God has revealed himself...as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit" (Article 2) — without reciting or subscribing the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed's text.

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 6(a)
fields.note: The statement says: "All who repent and believe on Christ as Saviour and Lord are to be baptized. Thus they declare to the world that they have died with Christ and that they also have been raised with Him to walk in newness of life" (Article 6(a), Baptism in Water).

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 2
fields.note: The statement says: "The one true God has revealed himself as the eternally self-existent 'I AM,' the Creator of heaven and earth" (Article 2).

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 2 (The One True God)
fields.note: The statement says: "The one true God has revealed himself as the eternally self-existent 'I AM,' the Creator of heaven and earth and the Redeemer of mankind. He has further revealed himself as embodying the principles of relationship and association as Father, Son and Holy Spirit" (Article 2). Article 2 of the Assemblies of God statement was written in 1916 partly to settle this question against the Oneness position within the movement.

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 7
fields.note: The statement says: "This experience is distinct from and subsequent to the experience of the new birth" (Article 7, The Baptism in the Holy Spirit).

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 7-8
fields.note: The statement says the baptism in the Holy Spirit brings "the bestowment of the gifts and their uses in the work of the ministry" (Article 7), and that speaking in tongues "is the same in essence as the gift of tongues" (Article 8) — both treating the New Testament gifts as continuing.

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 12
fields.note: The statement says: "Divine healing is an integral part of the gospel. Deliverance from sickness is provided for in the Atonement, and is the privilege of all believers" (Article 12, Divine Healing).

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 14
fields.note: The statement says: "The second coming of Christ includes the rapture of the saints...followed by the visible return of Christ with His saints to reign on the earth for one thousand years" (Article 14, The Millennial Reign of Christ).

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 5(a)
fields.note: The statement says: "being justified by grace through faith, man becomes an heir of God according to the hope of eternal life" (Article 5(a), Conditions to Salvation) — grace-through-faith justification, though the Statement does not itself use forensic-imputation vocabulary.

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 5(a); Article 6(a)
fields.note: The statement ties new birth to faith alone — "By the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Spirit, being justified by grace through faith, man becomes an heir of God" (Article 5(a)) — and separately describes water baptism as something believers undergo to "declare to the world" a death and resurrection already true of them (Article 6(a)), i.e. testimony rather than the means of the new birth.

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 1
fields.note: The statement says: "The Scriptures, both the Old and New Testaments, are verbally inspired of God and are the revelation of God to man, the infallible, authoritative rule of faith and conduct" (Article 1). The Assemblies of God's Statement affirms verbal inspiration and infallibility; 'inerrancy' as a term is more recent than the movement.

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 1
fields.note: The statement says: "The Scriptures, both the Old and New Testaments, are verbally inspired of God" (Article 1). The article does not itself enumerate the sixty-six books or address the deuterocanon; the Protestant canon is the Assemblies of God's settled practice rather than a point this article argues.

fields.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 1; Article 7
fields.note: The statement says Scripture is "the infallible, authoritative rule of faith and conduct" (Article 1) and describes the baptism in the Holy Spirit as bringing "the bestowment of the gifts and their uses in the work of the ministry" (Article 7) — continuing gifts operating alongside, not replacing, Scripture's stated authority.
